# Solutions 04 (Topic 1) — Tutorial 01: Generative Modelling, EDA & SLR

*Questions: [`../04-tutorial-caschools-slr.md`](../04-tutorial-caschools-slr.md).*

> Marking scheme: **70% for correct procedures, 30% for correct answers.**

---

## Problem 1 — The generative model and EDA

**(a)** "Generative modelling" means we assume the data were **generated by some underlying (stochastic)
mechanism**, and the regression is our **approximation of that data-generating process**. The
coefficients `b` are the **unknown true parameters** of that mechanism; we estimate them from a sample,
do inference to quantify our uncertainty, and use diagnostics to check whether the assumed mechanism is
plausible.

**(b)** **False.** An SLR is **not exact** — it includes a random error term. The correct model is
`Y_i = b0 + b1*X_i + e_i`. Without `e_i` every point would lie perfectly on the line, which never happens
with real (stochastic) data; the line gives only the **conditional average** `E[Y|X]`.

**(c)** `e_i` absorbs (1) the effect of **other explanatory variables not in the model** and (2) **pure
random noise**. We cannot observe it because it is defined relative to the **true** population line
(`b0, b1`), which is unknown — the best we can compute is the **residual** (from the estimated line),
which is only a stand-in for `e_i`.

**(d)** Any two of: (1) `ggpairs()` **picks the appropriate plot per variable type** (scatter,
box/violin, bar) automatically; (2) it shows each variable's **distribution on the diagonal**; (3)
instead of duplicating the mirrored scatterplots, it reports the **correlation coefficient** in the upper
triangle. Net: more information, less redundancy.

## Problem 2 — Fitting and inference for `read ~ income`

**(a)** **Correct:** "Each additional **\$1000** of district average income is **associated with** an
increase of about **1.94** points in the average reading score, on average across districts." The
"**raises**" version is wrong because it asserts **causation** from **observational** data — we can only
claim association.

**(b)** (i) **Yes, significant.** The 95% CI `(1.75, 2.13)` **excludes 0**, and `p < 0.05` — both say
reject `H0: b_income = 0`. (ii) The `lm` p-values come from **classical theoretical** approximations (the
t/Normal sampling distribution), **not** bootstrapping.

**(c)** The distribution of **`b̂1`, the estimator of the slope**. Not the distribution of `Y` (the
response scatter), nor of the true `b1` (a fixed unknown constant, not random), nor of `X` (treated as
fixed). The sampling distribution describes how the **estimate** varies from sample to sample.

**(d)** **Resample the observed districts with replacement**, each resample the **same size `n`** as the
data; refit `lm(read ~ income)` each time and store the slope — repeat **B = 10000** times to build
`boot_slope`. The spread of those 10000 slopes approximates the sampling distribution; a **90% CI** is
the **5th and 95th percentiles** of `boot_slope` (leaving 5% in each tail).
